rationale: B is stronger overall because it identifies the router as a scheduler and lifecycle manager, uses hysteresis and expected dwell to control swaps, protects interactive capacity with a reserved KV slice, reconciles its predictive memory ledger against the allocator, and specifies per-request resource ownership for leak-free cancellation. Its failure instrumentation is also better prioritized around OOM/fragmentation, swap-tail latency, stuck loads, thrash, and ledger drift. The main weakness is its boundary-only benchmark preemption: a long generation could still impose unacceptable interactive delay, so the design should support cooperative mid-generation abort and clean requeue when latency exceeds a bound. Its CPU KV offload should likewise be conditional on measured transfer cost and unified/system-memory pressure. A handles active benchmark cancellation more concretely, but its unconditional sticky period can block interactive work, its fixed-output canary is brittle for stochastic generation, and treating the router ledger rather than the real allocator as the source of truth is unsafe.
